description: The Athenian victory over Persia in 490 BC and why it became so celebrated in Greek memory.
content_html:
The Persian Empire and the Greek City-States

By the end of the sixth century BC, the Persian Empire had grown into the largest power the ancient world had ever seen. Under King Darius I, Persia controlled territories stretching from Egypt and Asia Minor in the west to India in the east. A number of Greek city-states along the coast of Asia Minor — Ionia — had come under Persian rule, and in 499 BC they rose in revolt against their Persian overlords. Athens sent ships to support the revolt. When it was crushed, Darius resolved to punish Athens.

The first major Persian expedition against mainland Greece came in 490 BC. The Persian fleet crossed the Aegean, attacked the island of Euboea, and then sailed to the bay of Marathon on the coast of Attica, roughly forty kilometres north-east of Athens. The choice of landing site was deliberate: Marathon offered a broad coastal plain suitable for the large Persian cavalry force. The Persians expected that either the Athenians would not dare fight, or that the cavalry would scatter any infantry foolish enough to engage in the open.

The Athenian Decision

Athens faced an existential crisis. The Persian army — estimates vary, but ancient sources suggest tens of thousands of infantry and cavalry — was far larger than the Athenian force of roughly nine or ten thousand hoplites. Athens sent a runner, Pheidippides, to Sparta to ask for military aid. The Spartans said they would help but could not march until the Carneia — a sacred festival of Apollo during which Spartan law forbade warfare — was over. They arrived too late to take part in the battle. Only the small city of Plataea sent a contingent, around a thousand hoplites, to stand alongside the Athenians.

The Athenian commanders debated what to do. The ten elected generals were divided: five voted to fight, five to wait. The tie was broken by the polemarch Callimachus, who sided with those who favoured action. The general most associated with the battle’s outcome was Miltiades, a man with first-hand experience of Persian methods of fighting, having served a Persian-controlled Chersonese on the Hellespont (the strait bordering the Gallipoli peninsula) before returning to Athens.

Key Fact

At Marathon in 490 BC, the Athenian generals were deadlocked five-to-five. Polemarch Callimachus cast the deciding vote to attack. General Miltiades, who had first-hand knowledge of Persian fighting methods from his time commanding the Chersonese on the Hellespont, devised the tactic that won the battle.

The Battle: Miltiades’ Tactic

Miltiades took a calculated risk. He deliberately thinned the Athenian centre to the minimum number of ranks needed to hold the line, while strengthening the wings on either side. His hoplite line was roughly a mile wide, matching the Persian deployment, but much weaker in the middle than a standard phalanx would be.

The Greeks charged at a run. Ancient sources describe the hoplites covering the distance at pace — about a mile, though this has been questioned — to close quickly with the Persians and reduce the time during which they were exposed to Persian archery. The Persians, who had expected a slow advance that their archers could pick apart, were surprised by the speed and weight of the Greek attack.

The plan worked as Miltiades intended. The thinned Greek centre was pushed back by the stronger Persian centre, but the stronger Greek wings drove their Persian opponents from the field. Rather than stopping to pursue the fleeing Persians on the flanks, the Greek wings then wheeled inward and attacked the victorious Persian centre from both sides at once. Caught between two closing lines of hoplites, the Persian centre collapsed. Many Persians were driven back to their ships on the shore; others were killed in the marshes at the edge of the plain.

After the Persian retreat, the victorious Athenian army faced a further danger. The Persian fleet had not been destroyed: it sailed around the Attic coast towards Athens, apparently in the hope of taking the city before the army could return. The hoplites marched back to Athens — in full armour, after a major battle — and arrived in time to man the walls before the Persian fleet appeared. The Persians, seeing that surprise was impossible, withdrew. According to later tradition, a herald ran ahead of the army to bring the news of victory: this is the origin of the modern marathon race, though the ancient version of the story attributes the run to Pheidippides, the man sent earlier to Sparta.

Visual Evidence: the Red-Figure Kylix

A red-figure kylix painted by the Triptolemos Painter — now in the collections of a major museum — shows a Greek and a Persian in single combat. The Greek figure is depicted in the distinctive equipment of a hoplite: round shield, spear, close-fitting helmet. The Persian figure wears clothing characteristic of eastern dress as the Athenians imagined it: a sleeved tunic, trousers and a soft Phrygian cap. The contrast is deliberate and loaded with meaning.

The kylix presents the conflict between Greece and Persia as a contest between two completely different kinds of fighter and, by extension, two different ways of life. The hoplite stands straight, well-armoured, visually ordered; the Persian is being pushed back, his posture less stable. Athenian vase painters returned to this theme repeatedly in the decades after Marathon and Salamis, reinforcing the ideological message that Greek courage and Greek equipment had triumphed over Persian numbers and eastern tyranny.

Key Fact

The red-figure kylix by the Triptolemos Painter shows a Greek hoplite and a Persian warrior in single combat. The visual contrast — armoured hoplite versus eastern-dressed Persian — was ideologically charged, presenting the Persian Wars as a victory of Greek order and courage over eastern tyranny.

Marathon mattered far beyond its immediate military result. Athens had stood alone against the greatest empire in the world — without Spartan help, with only the small Plataean contingent alongside — and had won. The psychological impact was enormous. Athenians who fought at Marathon were known as the Marathonomachai, the “Marathon fighters”, and for generations the battle was held up as proof of Athenian courage, discipline and democratic virtue.

The victory also shaped Athenian political confidence. It gave the democratic city-state, still relatively young in 490 BC, a founding military narrative: Athens had saved Greece when others would not. This narrative was deployed repeatedly in the fifth and fourth centuries to justify Athenian leadership of the Greek world. The burial mound of the Athenian dead — the soros — stood on the plain of Marathon and was a pilgrimage site for later generations.
exam_tip_html: For source analysis questions on the Triptolemos Painter kylix, go beyond saying “it shows a Greek and a Persian fighting” — describe specific visual details (the hoplite’s shield and spear, the Persian’s eastern dress) and explain what each detail tells us. Then analyse: what message was the painter trying to convey? Who was the audience? The biggest error in source analysis is description without analysis. For essay questions on why Marathon was significant, avoid just narrating events — argue for a specific significance (military, political, cultural) and use named sources and evidence to support your judgement.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • At Marathon in 490 BC, Miltiades thinned the Athenian centre to strengthen both wings; when the wings broke through, they wheeled inward and destroyed the Persian centre in a classic double envelopment.
  • Athens fought largely alone — Sparta arrived too late — which made the victory even more celebrated; the Marathonomachai became legendary figures in Athenian memory.
  • The Triptolemos Painter kylix showing a Greek defeating a Persian captures the ideological significance of the conflict: Greek discipline and equipment against Persian eastern tyranny.

practice_questions.text: Name the Athenian general who devised the tactics at the battle of Marathon.
Describe the red-figure kylix by the Triptolemos Painter and explain what it suggests about Athenian attitudes towards the Persians.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a specific visual detail (Greek hoplite in round shield and helmet / Persian in eastern dress including trousers and Phrygian cap / the two figures in combat); 1 mark for a second detail; 1 mark for explaining what it suggests (the contrast between hoplite order and eastern ‘barbarism’ was ideologically charged / Athenian artists repeatedly returned to this theme to celebrate Greek victory as a triumph of ordered courage over eastern tyranny).

practice_questions.text: Below is a paraphrase based on an ancient account of Marathon. The Athenian generals, knowing the Persians had cavalry and a far greater number of archers, decided to charge at a run to close the gap quickly. They deliberately strengthened the wings and thinned the centre. The Persian centre broke through the thin Athenian middle, but both Greek wings drove their opponents back, then turned inward to surround and destroy the Persian centre. Analyse this account as evidence for how Miltiades planned and won the battle of Marathon.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Uses specific details from the passage (running charge, thin centre, strong wings, the encirclement) to make analytical points about Miltiades’ tactical thinking; explains the significance of each detail (e.g. the run reduced time under fire from archers; the deliberate weakness in the centre was a trap, not a failure; the turning of the wings is the decisive moment); places in broader context. Secure: Identifies relevant features and makes valid analytical points; some explanation of significance. Developing: Describes the account rather than analysing it; limited explanation of significance. Emerging: Simple observations; little analysis.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Miltiades chose to thin the Athenian centre at Marathon.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per valid point with explanation, up to 4: the Greek line was about a mile wide, matching the Persian deployment, but Athenian numbers were insufficient to maintain full depth across the whole front / thinning the centre was necessary to ensure the wings were strong enough to break through / Miltiades expected the centre to be pushed back and planned for the wings to wheel inward afterwards / the tactic exploited Persian over-confidence and their expectation of a slow hoplite advance.

practice_questions.text: How far was the battle of Marathon a turning point in Athenian history? Use the sources you have studied to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument evaluating Marathon’s significance in military, political and cultural terms; uses named sources (the Triptolemos Painter kylix, the soros burial mound, literary accounts of the battle); considers other factors or perspectives (e.g. Marathon did not end the Persian threat; Salamis was arguably more decisive militarily); reaches a clear, supported judgement about the nature and extent of its significance. Secure: Clear argument addressing multiple dimensions of significance; uses some named sources; judgement present. Developing: Addresses significance in some detail but limited engagement with sources or counterarguments; judgement present but not fully developed. Emerging: Mostly narrative retelling of the battle; little argument; no clear judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Athens celebrated the victory at Marathon so strongly in the decades that followed.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains multiple reasons — Athens fought largely alone (without Sparta), the victory was against overwhelming odds, it gave the young democracy a founding military narrative, the Marathonomachai became legendary, the soros was a visible monument; connects these to the uses of Marathon in later Athenian politics; uses named sources. Secure: Clear explanation with relevant points developed; some use of sources. Developing: Basic explanation; limited development. Emerging: Vague; few specific points.

knowledge_checks.q: In which year did the battle of Marathon take place?
Which Athenian general devised the tactic of thinning the centre to strengthen the wings at Marathon?
The communal burial mound of the Athenian dead at Marathon, which became a pilgrimage site, was known as the _____.
Athens sent a runner named Pheidippides to Sparta to ask for help; the Spartans said they could not march until the _____ was over.
Match each person to their role at Marathon.
right: the runner sent to ask Sparta for help
the general who devised the winning tactics
the polemarch who cast the deciding vote to fight

flashcard_questions.q: When was the battle of Marathon?
What was Miltiades' key tactical decision at Marathon?
flashcard_questions.a: He thinned the Athenian centre and strengthened both wings to allow envelopment.

flashcard_questions.q: Why did the Athenian hoplites charge at a run at Marathon?
flashcard_questions.a: To close quickly with the Persians and reduce exposure to Persian archery.

flashcard_questions.q: Who cast the deciding vote to fight at Marathon?
Why did Sparta not fight at Marathon?
flashcard_questions.a: They were observing the Carneia, a sacred festival of Apollo that forbade warfare until it ended.

flashcard_questions.q: What city sent hoplites to fight alongside Athens at Marathon?
What was the soros at Marathon?
flashcard_questions.a: The communal burial mound of the Athenian dead, a monument on the plain.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the Triptolemos Painter kylix depict?
flashcard_questions.a: A Greek hoplite and a Persian warrior in single combat.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the ideological message of Athenian vase paintings showing Greeks fighting Persians?
flashcard_questions.a: Greek order and courage triumphed over Persian numbers and eastern tyranny.
The 'Marathon fighters' — Athenian veterans celebrated as heroes for generations.

flashcard_questions.q: What did the Persian fleet try to do after the army was defeated at Marathon?
flashcard_questions.a: Sail around to Athens, hoping to take the city before the army returned.

glossary_terms.definition: The Athenian war-archon who held a casting vote in military decisions; at Marathon, Callimachus cast the deciding vote in favour of attacking the Persians.
The Athenian general who devised the tactical plan at Marathon: thinning the centre to strengthen the wings, enabling the victorious wings to wheel inward and encircle the Persian centre.
A shallow, wide-mouthed Greek drinking cup, often decorated with painted scenes; red-figure examples showing Greeks and Persians in combat are evidence of how Athenians commemorated the Persian Wars.
The communal burial mound raised over the Athenian dead at Marathon, which stood on the plain as a permanent memorial and pilgrimage site.
